pages.hook: In the USA, people ask for your name and phone number all the time, at the doctor, at a restaurant and at the gym. Spelling it well saves a lot of trouble.

mythfact.s: The letter Z is usually “zee” in American English.
mythfact.why: In the USA it is “zee”. In British English it is “zed”.

mythfact.s: In phone numbers, Americans often say “oh” for the number 0.
mythfact.why: Both “zero” and “oh” are common: 5-0-5 can sound like “five oh five”.

mythfact.s: A normal US phone number has 15 digits.
mythfact.why: It has 10 digits: a 3-digit area code plus 7 more.

mythfact.s: Seattle is a city in the state of Washington.
mythfact.why: Seattle is in Washington state, in the northwest of the USA.

mythfact.s: In English, you must never say “D as in dog”.
mythfact.why: It is a very normal way to help someone hear a letter.

decode.q: What is the last name on the form?

lines: Hi, this is Mei from the gym.
Your name is spelled D-A-N-I-E-L, right?

opts: To check the spelling of a name
decode.why: She asks if the name is spelled D-A-N-I-E-L.

compare.br: In Brazil, people often say the phone number in pairs, like “nove, oito...”, and names are spelled less often.
compare.us: In the USA, people say each digit alone and often spell names, because there are many spellings: Ann or Anne, Jon or John.
compare.tip: Say the letters slowly and use a word if needed: “B as in boy”.
compare.ask: Spell your first name in English, letter by letter.

quiz.why: Say the letters one by one.

pages.title: Reading quest — My name is not easy · part 1
text: My name is Daniel, and I live in Seattle. In my country, my name is easy. In English, people sometimes write “Danyel” or “Daniell”. So I learned to **spell** it.

Last week I went to the gym. The woman at the desk asked, “**Can I have your name, please?**” I said, “**It’s Daniel**.” She asked, “**How do you spell that?**” I said, “**D-A-N-I-E-L**.” She smiled and said, “**Got it!**”

Then she asked for my **phone number**. I said, “It’s five-five-five, one-two-three-four.” She wrote it down. “**Is that your cell phone?**” she asked. “**Yes, it is**,” I said. “You’re all set. **Have a nice day!**”

opts: Spelling a name and a phone number
fast.why: Daniel spells his name at the gym.

scan.q: Where does the writer live?
How does he spell his name?
What does the woman say at the end?

tf.s: The writer lives in Seattle.
The woman at the gym asks for his name.
He has a house phone, not a cell phone.
tf.why: She asks “Is that your cell phone?” and he says yes.

tf.s: The rhyme “A Was an Apple Pie” is from Brazil.

order: The woman asks for his name.

ctx.sent: People write “Danyel” and I learned to spell it.
opts: say the letters of a word
ctx.why: Spell = say or write the letters.

ctx.sent: She wrote it down.
ctx.why: Write down = put on paper.

ctx.sent: It is a habit for me.
ctx.why: A habit is a regular action.

pages.title: Reading quest — My name is not easy · part 2
text: At home I remembered an old English rhyme, “A Was an Apple Pie”. It is from England and it is very old: the first mention is from 1671. Each **letter** of the **alphabet** does something to a pie: A bites it, B bakes it, C cuts it. Children learn the ABC with this rhyme.
Now I have a new habit. When people cannot hear a letter, I say, “B as in boy” or “D as in dog”. Spelling is not hard. It just needs time and a calm voice.

text: My name is Daniel, and I live in Seattle. In my country, my name is easy. In English, people sometimes write “Danyel” or “Daniell”. So I learned to **spell** it.

Last week I went to the gym. The woman at the desk asked, “**Can I have your name, please?**” I said, “**It’s Daniel**.” She asked, “**How do you spell that?**” I said, “**D-A-N-I-E-L**.” She smiled and said, “**Got it!**”

Then she asked for my **phone number**. I said, “It’s five-five-five, one-two-three-four.” She wrote it down. “**Is that your cell phone?**” she asked. “**Yes, it is**,” I said. “You’re all set. **Have a nice day!**”

At home I remembered an old English rhyme, “A Was an Apple Pie”. It is from England and it is very old: the first mention is from 1671. Each **letter** of the **alphabet** does something to a pie: A bites it, B bakes it, C cuts it. Children learn the ABC with this rhyme.
Now I have a new habit. When people cannot hear a letter, I say, “B as in boy” or “D as in dog”. Spelling is not hard. It just needs time and a calm voice.
